transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-10
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~41 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Orion Head of ML), Priya Desai (CTO), Marco Ruiz (Platform Eng)

Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect): Discussed unit economics of Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Focus on per-token pricing, batching and KV/prefix caching levers, reserved capacity commitments, and Orion's budget windows. Agreed to share pricing sheet and run benchmarks.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros? We'll focus on cost per unit and how hosting vs dedicated vs private changes the economics.
[00:18] Liam (Orion): Yeah hi, Liam here. We're evaluating models for a customer-facing assistant; traffic is spiky, budget is a concern.
[00:25] Priya (Orion): Priya here. Security & data residency are requirements but cost is the blocker initially.
[00:32] Marco (Orion): Marco - platform, I care about integration and autoscaling.
[00:36] Maya: Great. Ethan from our infra team will cover batching, caching, and quantization levers.
[00:42] Ethan (Redwood SE): Hey all. Quick note: when we talk per-token, there are multiple levers. Hosted is simplest - pay per-token at retail rates. Dedicated gives you reserved throughput for lower per-token effective cost once you amortize the GPU pool. Private adds ops overhead but can lower compute unit costs if you have capex.
[01:10] Liam: Can you give a concrete example? We estimate 50M tokens/month initially but could double. Our monthly budget is roughly $10k to start, ideally <$50k in steady state.
[01:25] Ethan: Sure. Rough numbers, depending on model family: Hosted retail might be $0.0006-0.002 per token for large-gen models, embeddings different; dedicated reserved capacity can drop effective per-token by 30-60% depending on utilization and batching. If you run at 50% GPU utilization, your amortized cost is higher.
[01:50] Maya: To add, we offer reserved tiers—monthly/annual commits—that reduce unit price. Also we recommend workarounds: prefix caching for repeated system prompts, KV cache reuse in session flows, and batching for background bulk tasks.
[02:12] Priya: That batching bit—how much does it hurt latency for interactive chat? Our SLO is p95 < 600ms for short-turn queries.
[02:22] Ethan: Interactive latency is sensitive. For live chat we use micro-batching with strict latency windows. You can set policies: target latency SLOs, and we trade off batching aggressiveness to meet p95. For 600ms SLO, you might only batch a few requests or rely on caching to avoid model run when possible.
[02:45] Marco: How does KV cache help? Sometimes users re-open conversations and we want continuity without re-sending the whole context.
[02:53] Ethan: KV cache stores transformer key/value states so you avoid recomputing prefix tokens. That reduces compute per turn and thus per-token cost because you only generate new tokens. We also have prefix caching for static system prompts. In hosted, cache hits are transparent; in Dedicated/Private, you can tune cache sizes and eviction.
[03:15] Liam: Any gotchas—like it doesn't work with certain quantized runtimes?
[03:20] Ethan: Good question. Some extreme quantization modes can complicate KV serialization across instances; we validate model variants. There's often a small engineering lift for private deployments to ensure caching serialization is robust.
[03:36] Maya: Also worth noting model selection: smaller families + instruction-tuning or distilled variants can reduce cost if they meet quality bar. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and model choices per workload.
[03:52] Priya: About private: we have an air-gapped pilot possibility. Ops cost there—how do we estimate? Is it mostly infra and our team's time?
[04:02] Ethan: Right, private adds ops: provisioning GPUs, networking, KMS, and monitoring. If you run on-prem, you absorb hardware depreciation and ops headcount; per-token compute cost may be lower, but TCO depends on utilization. We can surface a TCO model - we do this in pilots.
[04:22] Liam: For budgeting, we need a simple per-token comparison table: hosted list price, committed dedicated per-token, and an illustrative private TCO per-token at 60% utilization.
[04:33] Maya: We'll send that. Also we'll include examples of batching and cache savings for a conversational workflow vs. pure generation.
[04:44] Marco: Integration question: do we need to change our client SDK to get batching benefits?
[04:50] Ethan: For server-side batching, you don't change the client much; our gateway aggregates compatible requests. For client-side batching (e.g., bulk embedding jobs) you can use our batch APIs. For best results, instrument trace headers so we can map costs to routes.
[05:12] Priya: SLA-wise, if we go dedicated for a critical customer, do you provide latency guarantees?
[05:18] Maya: Yes, Dedicated has SLA-backed latency and uptime targets. Private SLAs are negotiated. Hosted offers best-effort but has strong observed performance metrics.
[05:27] Liam: Competitors offer committed use discounts too—how is Redwood different?
[05:31] Maya: We focus on inference economics with tooling: per-route cost breakdown, live recommendations (e.g., switch to a quantized variant for background workloads), and automated fallbacks across variants/regions to keep apps online.
[05:46] Liam: Example: If we have customer A with strict PII and need VPC, we'd consider Private, right? But cost-wise maybe dedicate?
[05:55] Ethan: For PII, Dedicated with VPC and customer-managed keys might be sufficient. Private is for air-gapped/regulatory needs. Dedicated gives isolation plus lower unit cost at scale without full ops burden.
[06:10] Marco: How do you handle model rollouts and experiments? If we test 2 models, do costs double?
[06:18] Ethan: We support canary and A/B; you can route a percentage of requests to cheaper model variants. Costs scale with traffic routed. We also have quality monitoring so you can correlate cost vs. quality.
[06:34] Priya: Back to concrete numbers: you mentioned 30-60% savings on dedicated—what assumptions?
[06:40] Ethan: That range assumes you commit to a monthly pool, maintain >=70% utilization, and use batching + caching aggressively. If utilization is low or you need many small, low-latency endpoints, savings shrink.
[06:58] Maya: Another lever is tokenization and prompt engineering - shorter prompts, summarization, retrieval-augmented flows reduce tokens per call. We can share a best-practice doc.
[07:09] Liam: We'd like an example calculation for our 50M tokens: hosted list price, dedicated with 12-month commit at 70% util, and private at 60% util.
[07:20] Maya: We'll draft that. Also we'll include embedding vs generation splits — embeddings cost differently.
[07:30] Marco: For benchmarking, what's needed from our side? Sample prompts, concurrency profile, and a traffic trace?
[07:36] Ethan: Exactly. Prefer a 7-day trace if possible, plus sample prompt sets for worst-case and typical flows. We'll run a perf run that mimics your concurrency distribution.
[07:48] Priya: Security docs—SOC2, ISO, SAML, KMS integrations—can you share those?
[07:54] Maya: Yes, we'll attach our security pack and SOC2 summary. For Private we can include deployment hardening notes.
[08:02] Liam: What's the minimum commitment for Dedicated? Is there a way to start small?
[08:07] Maya: We have smaller reserved tiers and trial credits for a Pilot Dedicated pool. You can start with a small commit and expand.
[08:15] Marco: Are there burst options for handling spikes?
[08:18] Ethan: Yes - burst buckets and cross-region fallback. That increases cost on the margin but preserves SLAs.
[08:26] Liam: Quick question on metering: do you charge tokens generated plus tokens input? We need to reconcile with our internal analytics.
[08:32] Maya: Yes, pricing typically counts both input and output tokens. Our console shows token breakdown by route and model.
[08:39] Priya: Any hidden costs—eg, network, egress, KMS?
[08:43] Ethan: For hosted, egress and KMS usage may add costs depending on region and KMS provider. For private, those are yours. We'll show a TCO with those line items.
[08:56] Liam: For ROI, we need to know at what monthly token volume Dedicated becomes cheaper than Hosted.
[09:02] Ethan: It depends on model and your latency SLOs, but ballpark for large-gen models, often in mid-seven-figures tokens per month to fully amortize without commits; with a modest commit, you can see savings at 50-200M tokens/month. We'll calculate with your 50M baseline.
[09:24] Maya: Let's move to prompts/examples—maybe run through a quick example of caching & batching impact.
[09:30] Ethan: Sure - imagine a chat flow where system prompt is 1k tokens, user asks for a short reply 20 tokens. If you have KV cache, you avoid re-encoding the 1k each turn. So compute is reduced by ~95% for subsequent turns. If you don't have caching, that 1k is re-sent and re-computed each time. With batching for background tasks, embedding jobs can be grouped into 128-item batches to amortize startup.
[10:01] Marco: How often do we see cache hit rates in real apps?
[10:04] Ethan: Varies. For session-based assistants, 60-80% for short re-turns if sessions persist; for ephemeral queries lower. We'll model different hit-rate scenarios.
[10:14] Priya: If we use retrieval augmentation, does that change tokens dramatically?
[10:18] Ethan: Retrieval can increase input tokens, but it improves quality and may reduce number of model calls via better concision. It's a tradeoff. Redwood Optimize can run sims.
[10:30] Liam: About model variants — if we switch to a 4-bit quantized variant for background summarization, is the quality gap measurable?
[10:36] Ethan: Often small for summarization tasks; we recommend running eval sets. Quantization reduces VM memory footprint and may speed throughput, lowering per-token cost. We surface quality/regression metrics.
[10:50] Maya: Any legal/procurement blockers we should be aware of?
[10:53] Priya: Data residency rules for EU customers, plus our procurement needs standard terms.
[10:58] Maya: We'll share our procurement template and regional options.
[11:03] Liam: Ok, let's recap next steps.
[11:07] Maya: Recap: we'll send pricing comparison and a TCO calc for 50M tokens; Ethan will provide a benchmarking plan and perf run template; Priya will share prompts and traffic; we schedule a technical deep-dive with infra next week.
[11:20] Marco: Sounds good.
[11:22] Priya: One more—do you have a time to review security docs with our security lead?
[11:26] Maya: Yes, we'll set that up.
[11:29] Liam: Thanks all.
[11:31] Maya: Thanks, meeting over.

End of transcript.
